def tidy(ax, grid="y"):
    for side in ("top", "right"):
        ax.spines[side].set_visible(False)
    for side in ("left", "bottom"):
        ax.spines[side].set_color(RULE)
    ax.tick_params(colors=MUTED)
    if grid:
        ax.grid(axis=grid, color=GRID, lw=0.8)
    ax.set_axisbelow(True)

Teaching with Rush Hour Project, phase 2: how does the student plan? (11/19 - 11/24/26)¶

Phase 1 (p1_summary.ipynb) ended with a simulated student that starts where people do and learns at their rate, which was enough to compare teachers. But that student only ever plays by intuition: one sample from its policy network per move. AND-OR's backward reasoning (Olieslagers et al. 2023) taught it in pretraining and then disappeared. People plan, and how they plan is what a teacher's help would have to fit into. Phase 2 asks:

  1. What would a planning student look like - backward (AND-OR), forward (simulating moves ahead), or both?
  2. What makes a student human-like, beyond the solve rate and moves / optimal that phase 1 fitted?
  3. How do people actually combine ways of choosing a move, and does that change as they learn?
Notebook What it covers
p2.1_deliberation.ipynb Backward planning alone: AND-OR ordered by the network, against people
p2.2_forward_planning.ipynb Forward planning (novelty, relevance, the value head); forward + backward together; planners in the session; calibrating every planner to people's start; people's move times; a move-by-move mixture of modes; the two-mode student
p2.3_human_likeness.ipynb People against the models move by move: optimal moves by distance, revisits, car roles, slides, timing; fitting a soft memory to people's revisits

This notebook is the through-line: each section states the question, the answer, and where the evidence is. Its figures are rebuilt from the saved results (models/summary, models/sessions; see MODELS.md).

1. Measuring humanness: what tells models apart¶

(p2.3, sections 1-8) Solve rate and moves / optimal can be matched by very different solvers. So people and every candidate model were compared move by move on the 70 layouts people played: how often a move is optimal at each distance from the goal, how often they return to an earlier board or undo, where moved cars land, which cars in the AND-OR tree get moved, how far cars slide, and how long moves take.

  • Most measures track efficiency. At matched efficiency (solved attempts of 1.5-3 × optimal) every model makes optimal moves at about people's rate. What doesn't wash out is the shape by distance: people are better than every model in the middle of a puzzle, and the planners are too good near the goal (left).
  • People revisit and undo; the phase 1 student can't. At matched efficiency people return to an earlier board on 10% of moves and undo on 6%, like AND-OR. The intuition student's hard rule (never back to the last 10 boards) forbids both, and fits people's revisits worse than no memory at all (right).
  • People's memory is weak, not long: the best replacement lowers a move back to a recent board by β = 2 logits fading with a 1-move half-life (an undo about 30-40% less likely). This soft memory is used by every model below. People also put cars back where they had been on 40% of moves, more than any model, and rarely move cars outside the AND-OR tree (4.4% of moves, against 14.6% of legal moves).

2. Backward planning alone¶

(p2.1) The most direct planning student is AND-OR itself, with the network ordering its options (the dest head, with Gumbel noise; since 11/24 the policy head, section 7) instead of choosing at random.

on people's 70 layouts (first 10 trials) solved moves / optimal
people 0.87 about 2.8
AND-OR ordered by the trained network (γ 0.035) 0.70 people's level on 10-15-move puzzles; ≈1.1 on 6-move (people 1.8)
plain AND-OR (random order), same γ 0.63 ≈3.5
  • Efficiency at people's level, solving not: the long layouts defeat it (about 0.5 solved against people's 0.8 on 13- and 15-move puzzles), and not because of giving up - with none it still solves only 0.77.
  • The network mostly buys efficiency: ordering AND-OR's options cuts moves / optimal from ≈3.5 to ≈2.5.
  • And from section 1, AND-OR's style is human in one way the intuition student isn't (it revisits and undoes), but it is too good near the goal. Backward planning alone is not the student.

3. Forward planning, then forward and backward together¶

(p2.2, sections 1-2b) A forward planner simulates short rollouts from the board with the policy and judges where they end.

  • Novelty (width-based planning: credit for car placements the attempt hasn't had) halves moves / optimal for every network; the dest head's relevance adds nothing, even with uniform proposals (the dest head has since been removed); the network's experience enters through the moves it proposes. The value head (predicted moves to go) is weak alone and useful as a tie-breaker.
  • But novelty is not human (p2.3, section 9): people return cars to earlier spots constantly, which novelty forbids. Fitted to people's revisits, the planner wants no novelty - rollouts judged by the value head alone, with the soft memory.
  • Forward and backward complement each other: 4 policy rollouts + 4 AND-OR passes, judged alike by the value head (best of 8), beat 8 of either kind for every network (start network: 4.88 moves / optimal against 5.27 and 5.31). Its excess undos came from fresh AND-OR passes; letting the memory judge the candidates fixes them (5.4% undos, 9.6% returns; people 5.6%, 9.7%).
  • One lapse rate γ for both directions fits as well as two, and the best γ falls over people's session (0.03 → 0.01): deeper thought with practice, as van Opheusden et al. found. But γ cannot fix the skill shape (99% optimal near the goal against people's 87%; 31-43% mid-puzzle against 54%), and neither can giving the planner the networks the intuition session learned. Networks trained on the planner's own play help a little (53% optimal 7-9 moves out by trials 46+, against 49%; people 59%).

4. Which planner can start where people do?¶

(p2.2, section 2c) The planner played in the session started near-optimal (1.44 moves / optimal against people's 2.76) and had nothing to learn. So every planner was calibrated to people's first 10 trials the way phase 1 chose its start (surrender.py: the session's test puzzles at people's lengths, giving up applied at the session's scale). Families: best of 8; forward rollouts alone; flat (Collins et al.'s novices: the policy's top few moves looked at one move deep, a softmax over the value head's moves to go); flat + a checking rollout; an impasse switch (flat, with an AND-OR plan at an impasse); and the forward and two-mode students (section 6).

(hs, hs_se), (hr, hr_se), first10 = sr.human_target(10)
edges, rates, _ = hd.surrender_hazard()
test_puzzles = sr.puzzle_set("test")


def calibrate(df, scale=0.3):
    rows = []
    for c, d in df.groupby("config", sort=False):
        att = {n: [None if m != m else int(m) for m in x.moves] for n, x in d.groupby("puzzle")}
        ps, pr = sr.predict(att, test_puzzles, first10, edges, rates, scale, True)
        rows.append({"config": c, "solved": ps, "moves / optimal": pr,
                     "misfit": ((ps - hs) / hs_se) ** 2 + ((pr - hr) / hr_se) ** 2})
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)


def family(c):
    for prefix, name in [("intuition, hard", "intuition (phase 1's start)"), ("intuition, soft", None),
                         ("best of 8", "best of 8 (4 + 4)"), ("forward", "forward rollouts"),
                         ("flat+check", "flat + check"), ("flat", "flat"), ("two-mode", "impasse switch"),
                         ("lean", "forward / two-mode")]:
        if c.startswith(prefix):
            return name


mixed = pd.read_csv(os.path.join(SUMMARY, "planner_start_fit.csv"))
mixed["config"] = "best of 8, γ " + mixed.gamma.astype(str)
cal = pd.concat([calibrate(mixed)] + [calibrate(pd.read_csv(os.path.join(SUMMARY, f))) for f in
                 ("forward_start_fit.csv", "flat_start_fit.csv", "two_mode_start_fit.csv", "lean_start_fit.csv")],
                ignore_index=True)
cal["family"] = cal.config.map(family)
cal = cal[cal.family.notna()]

ax.errorbar([hr], [hs], xerr=[hr_se], yerr=[hs_se], fmt="s", color=PEOPLE, ms=7, capsize=3, label="people, trials 1-10")

  • Anything that deliberates on every move starts too good. Best of 8 stalls near 1.9 moves / optimal at any γ - choosing among candidates is itself what makes a student efficient. Forward rollouts fit only with 2 of them; flat fits only when its choice is so noisy that the value head barely counts; a sharp flat choice gets stuck in loops (93% of the moves in its failed attempts go back to a board already seen). The impasse switch rescues the sharp choice but starts too efficient (best misfit 7.5).
  • Only intuition, and the two-mode student, start where people do. Phase 1's start (intuition with the hard memory) fits at 0.1; the two-mode student fits at 0.0-1.2 with weights near what people's moves show (section 5).

5. How people combine ways of choosing a move¶

(p2.2, section 2c) Two kinds of evidence from people themselves.

Move times. Most moves are fast (median 0.7 s; the first move of an attempt 2.9 s). Faster moves (for that person) are better: the fastest fifth is 92% optimal 2-3 moves from the goal and undoes 3.7% of the time, the slowest fifth 67% and 10.5%. Slow moves look like impasses, not careful choices. Over the session the share of slow moves stays at 15-17%; the gains are in fast moves. Hundreds of simulated steps per move (best of 8) are implausible at 0.7 s.

A move-by-move mixture. Every human move gets an exact probability under intuition (the policy) and flat planning (top 5 moves, value head, τ 1), and a sampled one under AND-OR (one pass, its first move). Each move is a mix of the three, with weights fitted per stage of the session, distance to the goal and move speed. The network is either the start network or, per stage, the intuition session's own network at that point.

  • Intuition is the base: 76-88% of moves in every breakdown.
  • Flat planning grows with practice, but only with a learned evaluator: 8% → 18% of moves with each stage's network (it rose for 27 of 37 people); with the start network it stays at 8-10%. It peaks mid-puzzle and lives in fast moves - a quick "propose a few, pick the one that looks closest", used more as the evaluator becomes worth consulting.
  • AND-OR is about a tenth of moves and does not grow. It is strongest near the goal and on slow moves (18% against 8% of other fast moves), plus the move after a slow first look at a puzzle (14%). It does not follow a loop (4%, below elsewhere: people who go in a circle retry the familiar move), and no plan is carried out after a slow move. People's backward reasoning looks like one deliberated move at a time - the paper's AND-OR model (one move per search), not a plan played to its end.

6. The forward and two-mode students¶

(p2.2, section 2c) forward.solve_lean turns the mixture into a student: each move it draws a mode - a one-move AND-OR deliberation (probability w_ao), flat planning (w_flat) or intuition - with the soft memory; optionally a deliberated opening. It keeps only what people's moves asked for: no rollouts, no plan following. Named for its modes: the two-mode student reasons forward (intuition and flat planning) and, now and then, backward (single AND-OR deliberations); the forward student is the same without AND-OR. (In the code they are one solver, forward.solve_lean / forward.LeanSolver, --lean, with w_ao 0 for the forward student; saved runs and tables keep the name lean_*.) forward.LeanSolver plays it in the calibrated session with the flat share rising over 30 trials, as people's did: the two-mode student (flat 8% → 18%, AND-OR 10%, the opening) and the forward student (no AND-OR; flat 18% → 28%, which is what it needs to start where people do).

The two-mode student move by move. The page below (visualization/p2_two_mode/two_mode_moves.html, built by python experiments/two_mode_animation.py) steps through one attempt on a 10-move layout of people's: for each move, the random draw that picks the mode against the weights (AND-OR 18%, flat 6%, intuition the rest, at the start of a session; the opening always AND-OR), then what that mode weighed - intuition's probabilities, flat planning's five candidates with the value network's moves to go, or AND-OR's plan, of which only the first move is played. The replay uses solve_lean's own random draws and is checked to play the same moves. The attempt was picked to show every mode, so it has more planned moves than a typical one.

def session_curve(path):
    d = json.load(open(path))
    rows = []
    for lo, hi in [(1, 9), (10, 27), (28, 45), (46, 72)]:
        es = [e for r in d.values() for e in r if lo <= e["trial"] <= hi]
        won = [e for e in es if e["solved"]]
        rows.append({"trials": f"{lo}-{hi}", "solved": np.mean([e["solved"] for e in es]),
                     "moves / optimal (solved)": np.mean([e["moves"] / e["distance"] for e in won])})
    return pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("trials")


t_people = hd.trials()
people_curve = []
for lo, hi in [(1, 9), (10, 27), (28, 45), (46, 72)]:
    g = t_people[t_people.trial.between(lo, hi)]
    w = g[g.solved]
    people_curve.append({"trials": f"{lo}-{hi}", "solved": g.groupby("subject").solved.mean().mean(),
                         "moves / optimal (solved)": (w.moves / w.distance).groupby(w.subject).mean().mean()})
curves = {"people": pd.DataFrame(people_curve).set_index("trials"),
          "phase 1 student (intuition)": session_curve(os.path.join(fm.ARCHIVE_RUN, "sessions.json")),
          "two-mode": session_curve(os.path.join(paths.SESSIONS, "lean_people_all_m10_ao", "no_teacher",
                                                         "sessions.json")),
          "forward": session_curve(os.path.join(paths.SESSIONS, "lean_people_all_m10_noao", "no_teacher",
                                                            "sessions.json"))}
paired, speople = {}, None
for name, run in [("two-mode", "lean_people_all_m10_ao"), ("forward", "lean_people_all_m10_noao")]:
    f, speople = fm.summarize_learning(pd.read_csv(os.path.join(SUMMARY, f"lean_snapshots_{run}.csv")), fm.SNAP_STAGES)
    paired[name] = f[[r.snapshot == fm.SNAP_OF[r.stage] for r in f.itertuples()]].set_index("stage")
C = {"people": PEOPLE, "phase 1 student (intuition)": "#8a8a85", "two-mode": "#e6550d",
     "forward": "#e6a00d"}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(13, 3.4))
for name, d in curves.items():
    axes[0].plot(range(4), d["moves / optimal (solved)"], "o-", color=C[name], label=name)
axes[0].set_xticks(range(4), curves["people"].index)
axes[0].set_xlabel("trials")
axes[0].set_title("Learning in the session: moves / optimal")
axes[0].legend(fontsize=7)

                       (axes[2], "optimal 7-9", "Human layouts: optimal 7-9 from the goal")]:
    ax.plot(range(4), speople.loc[STAGES, col], "o-", color=PEOPLE, label="people")
    for name, d in paired.items():
        ax.plot(range(4), d.loc[STAGES, col], "o-", color=C[name], label=name)
    ax.set_xticks(range(4), [f"{s}\n({n})" for s, n in fm.SNAP_OF.items()])
    ax.set_xlabel("people's trials (the student's network after n)")

  • The two-mode student learns like people: 2.87 → 2.27 moves / optimal over the session (people 2.77 → 2.17), as well as phase 1's student, which was fitted to that curve - while also planning. The forward student stalls mid-session and loses accuracy near the goal as its flat share climbs. AND-OR earns its place, not as a solver but as occasional deliberated moves that let the flat share start low and rise.
  • The two-mode student is weaker than people at every distance on their layouts: 70-74% optimal 2-3 moves from the goal against people's 85-89%, and 30-34% at 7-9 against 48% → 59% - while matching people's efficiency on the session's puzzles. Part of this is the layouts (they offer more legal moves and fewer good ones than pool puzzles of the same length), but not the near-goal part: the start network's intuition is only 61% optimal 2-3 moves out even on the session's own puzzles. Phase 1 fitted the student's overall efficiency, and it got there by being middling everywhere, where people are near-perfect close to the goal and better mid-puzzle.

7. Does the two-mode student learn like people?¶

(p2.2, section 2c) Beyond the efficiency curve: the curve in finer blocks, the gain per puzzle length, giving up and restarting, how much individuals differ, and the snapshots on people's layouts by stage. People's figures are means over people (the students' over the 8 students); the session plays pool puzzles at people's lengths.

STAGE_BOUNDS = [(1, 9), (10, 27), (28, 45), (46, 72)]
stage_of = lambda x: next(f"{a}-{b}" for a, b in STAGE_BOUNDS if a <= x <= b)


def session_records(run):
    """One row per puzzle of a session run (every student), with its stage of people's session."""
    d = json.load(open(os.path.join(paths.SESSIONS, run, "no_teacher", "sessions.json")))
    e = pd.DataFrame([dict(x, subject=s) for s, rec in d.items() for x in rec])
    return e.assign(stage=e.trial.map(stage_of), ratio=e.moves / e.distance)


people_t = hd.trials()
people_t = people_t[people_t.trial <= 72].assign(stage=lambda t: t.trial.map(stage_of),
                                                 ratio=lambda t: t.moves / t.distance,
                                                 restarted=lambda t: t.attempts > 1)
LEARNERS = {"people": people_t, "two-mode": session_records("lean_people_all_m10_ao"),
            "forward": session_records("lean_people_all_m10_noao")}
LEARNER_COLORS = {"people": INK, "two-mode": "#e6550d", "forward": "#e6a00d"}


def by_stage(d):
    """Per stage: means over individuals (people or students) of solving, giving up, restarting and moves / optimal
    on solved puzzles, the spread of moves / optimal across individuals, and moves / optimal per puzzle length."""
    rows = {}
    for st, g in d.groupby("stage", sort=False):
        w = g[g.solved]
        each = w.ratio.groupby(w.subject).mean()
        r = {"solved": g.groupby("subject").solved.mean().mean(),
             "gave up": g.groupby("subject").surrendered.mean().mean(),
             "restarted": g.groupby("subject").restarted.mean().mean() if "restarted" in g else 0.0,
             "moves / optimal": each.mean(), "sd across individuals": each.std()}
        for length, gl in w.groupby("distance"):
            r[f"length {length}"] = gl.ratio.groupby(gl.subject).mean().mean()
        rows[st] = r
    return pd.DataFrame(rows).T.loc[[f"{a}-{b}" for a, b in STAGE_BOUNDS]]


stages_table = pd.concat({k: by_stage(d) for k, d in LEARNERS.items()})
layouts = {}  # snapshots on people's 70 layouts, against the same stage of people
for name, run in [("two-mode", "lean_people_all_m10_ao"), ("forward", "lean_people_all_m10_noao")]:
    f, layout_people = fm.summarize_learning(pd.read_csv(os.path.join(SUMMARY, f"lean_snapshots_{run}.csv")),
                                             fm.SNAP_STAGES)
    layouts[name] = f[[r.snapshot == fm.SNAP_OF[r.stage] for r in f.itertuples()]].set_index("stage")
layouts = pd.concat({"people": layout_people, **layouts})[["optimal 2-3", "optimal 7-9", "moves / optimal", "board 2"]]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(15, 3.4))
for name, d in LEARNERS.items():  # (a) the efficiency curve in blocks of 9 trials
    w = d[d.solved].assign(block=lambda x: (x.trial - 1) // 9)
    curve = w.groupby(["block", "subject"]).ratio.mean().groupby("block").mean()
    axes[0].plot(curve.index * 9 + 5, curve.values, "o-", color=LEARNER_COLORS[name], label=name, ms=4)
axes[0].set_xlabel("trial")
axes[0].set_title("(a) moves / optimal, blocks of 9 trials")
lengths = [6, 10, 13, 15]  # (b) the gain from the first to the last stage, per puzzle length
for k, name in enumerate(LEARNERS):
    t = stages_table.loc[name]
    gain = [t.loc["1-9", f"length {L}"] - t.loc["46-72", f"length {L}"] for L in lengths]
    axes[1].bar(np.arange(4) + (k - 1) * 0.27, gain, 0.27, color=LEARNER_COLORS[name], label=name)
axes[1].set_xticks(range(4), [f"{L} moves" for L in lengths])
axes[1].set_title("(b) gain in moves / optimal, trials 1-9 to 46+")
for name in LEARNERS:  # (c) giving up, and people's restarts
    t = stages_table.loc[name]
    axes[2].plot(range(4), t["gave up"], "o-", color=LEARNER_COLORS[name], label=f"{name}: gave up")
axes[2].plot(range(4), stages_table.loc["people"]["restarted"], "o--", color=INK, label="people: restarted")
axes[2].set_xticks(range(4), [f"{a}-{b}" for a, b in STAGE_BOUNDS])
axes[2].set_xlabel("trials")
axes[2].set_title("(c) giving up and restarting")
for k, (name, d) in enumerate(LEARNERS.items()):  # (d) individuals' whole-session efficiency
    w = d[d.solved]
    each = w.ratio.groupby(w.subject).mean()
    jitter = np.random.default_rng(0).uniform(-0.15, 0.15, len(each))
    axes[3].scatter(k + jitter, each.values, s=14, color=LEARNER_COLORS[name], alpha=0.7)
axes[3].set_xticks(range(3), list(LEARNERS))
axes[3].set_title("(d) individuals: moves / optimal, whole session")
for ax in axes[:3]:
    ax.legend(fontsize=7)
for ax in axes:
    tidy(ax)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
display(stages_table.round(3))

  • Where the two-mode student learns like people
    • How much and how fast. On solved puzzles in the session, moves / optimal falls 2.87 → 2.27 (people 2.77 → 2.17): the same 0.60. In blocks of 9 trials both fall fast over the first ~30 trials and then flatten (a).
    • On which puzzles, roughly. Both gain little on 6-move puzzles and most on 13-move ones (b: people 3.40 → 2.24, the student 3.72 → 2.81). In between they differ: on 10-move puzzles the student gains half as much as people (0.47 against 0.94), on 15-move ones a little more (0.78 against 0.60).
    • On people's layouts, in proportion. Its snapshots there cut moves / optimal by 20% (3.52 → 2.81); people on the same layouts cut it by 17% (2.32 → 1.93).
    • Revisits stay human. About 7% of its moves undo the last one throughout, against people's 5-6% (revisit misfit 0.05-0.07 at every stage).
  • Where it doesn't
    • Giving up and restarting run the other way (c). People restart 13-20% of puzzles and give up more late in the session (12% → 16%), so their solve rate falls at the end (88% → 84%). The student never restarts, gives up less as it improves (8% → 6%), and solves a flat 82-84%. Nothing in the model tires or loses patience.
    • Its level on people's layouts is too low. It gains in proportion but from far below them: 70-72% optimal 2-3 moves from the goal against people's 85-89%, and 3.5 → 2.8 moves / optimal against 2.3 → 1.9. Its session curve matches people's only on the pool puzzles its start was calibrated on, which are easier than people's layouts 7+ moves from the goal (the same network, on pool puzzles of people's lengths: 8-15 points more often optimal there). A start calibrated on people's own layouts (round 2 epoch 5 by intuition, which matches their first attempts and their skill by distance) fixes the level, but in the session it barely learns at any multiplier or training mix (experiments/session_fit.py → session_fit.csv).
    • Individuals hardly differ (d). Across people, whole-session moves / optimal spreads widely (a standard deviation of 0.6-1.4 per stage); across the 8 students, 0.07-0.17. Every student starts from the same network and differs only by chance: there are no fast or slow learners.
    • Part of the learning is imposed. The flat share rising from 8% to 18% is a schedule taken from the mixture fit, not something the student finds. The forward student, with the same kind of schedule and no AND-OR, gains less and stalls mid-session (2.88 → 2.36), but how much of the two-mode student's gain is the network's and how much the schedule's hasn't been separated.
    • Mid-puzzle skill (accepted as a limitation for now): 31-34% optimal 7-9 moves from the goal against people's 48% → 59%.
  • So the defensible claim is narrower than "learns like people": the two-mode student reproduces how much people improve, how fast and on which puzzles, but not their level on their own layouts, their giving up and restarting, or how much they differ from each other. Caveats: one seed, 8 students per run; people's later stages have fewer people (not everyone played 72 trials).

A network without a dest head (11/24). The dest head existed to order AND-OR's options. Two tests showed the two-mode student doesn't need it:

  • Ordering. With the start network on people's 70 layouts, AND-OR ordered by the policy head plays its moves as well as AND-OR ordered by the dest head inside the two-mode student (44.3% against 43.4% of its moves optimal), and better when AND-OR plays every move (68% solved against 58%). A blocked move's policy score is the network's sense of that car going there, learned on boards where the move was legal. Random order is about 5 points worse.
  • Removing it. Round 1 of the apprentice retrained on the same data with no dest targets (gamma0.07_free_nodest) learns at the same pace; fitted to people's start the same way, its epoch 3 matches (misfit 0.2, giving up × 0.35). Its two-mode session (lean_people_all_m10_ao_nodest) gains 0.58 moves / optimal (dest head: 0.60; people: 0.60), and on people's layouts its snapshots gain 0.79 (dest head: 0.71). Its start there is no worse once both use the same ordering (3.61 against 3.57 moves / optimal); replays of one network differ by about 0.1 in skill misfit per stage.

So the student's network is now two heads, policy and value, and every session starts from that apprentice (paths.START; the dest-head start, used by every run of 11/19-11/24, is paths.DEST_START). It is still AND-OR's apprentice - it learned AND-OR's moves and distances - but no longer the order AND-OR tried its options in, which in round 1's plain AND-OR was random anyway. Phase 1's multiplier, hindsight and teacher threshold were fitted with the dest-head start and are kept.

The mode weights refitted (11/24). With AND-OR ordered by the policy head and the no-dest start (experiments/mode_mixture.py; the old fit is in summary/mode_mixture_dest/), people's moves fit AND-OR more often and flat planning about as often:

  • AND-OR: 18% of moves with the start network (was 10%), 14% → 20% over the stages (was 10% → 8%). It is still strongest near the goal (44% of moves 2-3 from it, was 34%) and on slow moves (22%, was 18%).
  • Flat planning: 6% → 18% over the first 30 trials with each stage's network (was 8% → 18%). Only the first stage changed, the only one scored with the new start.
  • Part of AND-OR's rise is the ordering itself: a policy-ordered pass most often opens with the policy's top move (on 67% of boards), so its weight partly measures people being sharper than the policy, not only reasoning backward.

The two-mode student now uses these weights (AND-OR 18%, flat 6% → 18%). Its start needs no change: with them, epoch 3 still matches people's first 10 trials (2.88 moves / optimal and 86% solved, against 2.76 ± 0.17 and 87%; misfit 0.8). In the session (lean_people_all_m10_ao_nodest_refit) it gains 0.47 moves / optimal at seed 0 and 0.56 at seed 1 (old weights: 0.58 at both; people: 0.60). Seed 0 dipped in trials 4-9 and recovered, so the difference is replay noise. On people's layouts its snapshots gain 0.76 (old weights: 0.79), with skill misfit 0.88, 0.69, 0.70, 0.71 by stage (old weights: 0.96, 0.76, 0.63, 0.70), and near the goal it is no better: 70-74% of moves 2-3 from the goal optimal, against people's 85-89%.

Two networks instead of one (11/24, p2.5_value_network). The policy and value heads shared a trunk, trained on both losses. Trained without the distance loss, the policy learns as fast and matches people's start at the same epoch; a value network trained on the distances alone judges as well; and the two-mode sessions with a separate policy network and value network gain as much (0.62 and 0.54 at two seeds, against 0.47 and 0.56; people 0.60), follow the rules the same way and fit people's layouts as well (within the noise of seeds and replays). The student is now two networks (paths.START): one learns to choose, the other to judge.

8. Where this leaves the student¶

phase 1's student the two-mode student
choosing a move a policy sample, every move a policy sample on most moves; flat planning (top 5 moves, value head) on 6% → 18%; a one-move AND-OR deliberation on 18% (both refitted 11/24), and on the first move of an attempt
memory of where it has been never back to the last 10 boards a soft, fading penalty fitted to people's revisits
what AND-OR does teaches it in pretraining the same, plus occasional single deliberated moves
the network policy, dest and value heads (the dest head ordered AND-OR) a policy network (which also orders AND-OR) and a separate value network (since 11/24)
starts where people do yes (misfit 0.1) yes (0.0-1.2)
learns like people yes (fitted) its efficiency gain: as much, as fast, on similar puzzles; not people's giving up, restarts or individual differences (section 7)
human-like move by move no revisits; no planning revisits like people; mixes modes as people's moves suggest

Open questions, in order:

  1. The shape of skill: people are near-perfect close to the goal (85-89%) and better mid-puzzle; the two-mode student is middling everywhere. Near the goal, a short lookahead that sees the exit ("goal in sight") or a sharper policy are candidates. Mid-puzzle, the gap no model closes, candidates are training the value head on the student's own flat choices; a rule for when each mode is used (the policy's uncertainty, the blocking chain people can see) instead of fixed odds; a flat share tied to how reliable the evaluator has become (Daw et al. 2005) rather than a schedule.
  2. What triggers a slow, deliberated move - not a loop; the opening is one trigger.
  3. The teachers again: phase 1's teachers (bayes4) were compared on the intuition student. Help that shows a move lands differently on a student that sometimes plans: does bayes4 still help, and does agency (ΔA) still decide when help pays?

Papers this phase drew on: Olieslagers et al. 2023 (AND-OR; people's data); van Opheusden et al. 2023 (expertise as deeper search); Collins et al. 2026 (novices plan flat and fast); Zhang et al. 2025 (the network decides what is considered); Lipovetzky & Geffner (width-based novelty); Daw, Niv & Dayan 2005, Lee et al. 2014, Keramati et al. 2011/2016, Kool et al. 2017, Lieder & Griffiths 2017, Callaway et al. 2022 (arbitration and metareasoning); Newell & Simon 1972, Anzai & Simon 1979 (means-ends analysis; strategies shifting with practice).
